doc.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022

title: Making a living now, working with Ada, 300 tunes since Covid
summary: Music careers are harder; he and his wife Ada Rovatti record remote parts and keep up with trends.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: I see. I’m glad you brought up Ada’s name, your wife, and I flashed to this little thing I’m going to run by you. Bassist — I don’t know if you know bassist Frank Tate but this goes back 21 years. But I asked him, the question I had for him was what’s it like to make a living as a professional musician. And his answer was, “Well I have a wife who has a real job so it’s not too bad.” So is it challenging for both of you to be in the music business or have you sort of worked out the mechanism?

Well you know like I said, I was lucky to come to New York when I did, wanting to be a freelance player because then there was a lot of work, studio work for those who lent themselves to that. You had to have a certain kind of personality and a certain kind of well rounded way of playing and like different styles of music. I just fit into that mindset pretty easily as did my brother and a lot of the studio musicians. But Broadway was happening — there’s problems there now with electronic orchestras taking over, an electronic conductor that when they move their hand the orchestra will move along with them. It’s gotten pretty insane. It was also an avid club date scene, so a lot of guys were

working all the time. But now it’s a concern. You know you really have to want to write, you really need to write to get some kind of writing checks under your belt, do your own projects, teach and play. It’s very hard to make a living just as a player. So things have changed a lot. And I think it’s been harder for her. It’s been lucky that we work together really well so we’ve done a lot of this stuff in this room. I was amazed — I started saving some of the sessions we’ve done just the last couple of years. Usually we have to do a solo, there might be some horn parts, she’s gotten really good at writing horn parts. I don’t really feel like doing it anymore. She went to Berklee. She’ll tell you, and she started arranging and she’s great at it, really fast, and gets it into the computer really quickly because I’m very slow at all that stuff. So I’m very lucky to have her. And we just work together really well. But we’ve done, since — once I started saving the sessions — and a lot of them were for people I don’t even know. Some were people I know but we get things from, you know, they find a way to get in touch with me and they send the files via email. We put them in Pro Tools and I put on headphones and off we go. It sounds — but literally since Covid there’s been close to 300 different tunes that I’ve played on. That’s just the last two or three years. And each of those are a solo. That’s what — it’s hard for me to wrap my head around that I have to come up with something each time. I try to play something a little different but it’s a challenge. And we always come up with something good because of the technology because like I said we can sculpt it to fit whatever is needed and we’re good at that you know because we get all different styles. And I spend a lot of time — I always have — I’m also a big listener so I try to stay up on things that are happening. I can’t completely stay up on it because it’s so involved now, all the social media, Tik Tok, all the crazy stuff that’s happening now to get your music out. I can’t begin to even follow that. But I like to read about it and just try to integrate some of it into my head. Maybe it’ll have some kind of effect on what we’re playing or writing.
